title: No verdict Saturday in trial of officers accused in death of Corey Rogers
article: After a long day of deliberation on Saturday, the jury still hasn't come to a decision in the trial of two special constables accused of criminal negligence causing the death of Corey Rogers.
Cheryl Gardner and Dan Fraser were booking officers the night of June 15, 2016, when Rogers was taken into the Halifax Regional Police Gottingen Street headquarters cells for public drunkenness.
He died that night of asphyxiation, choking on his own vomit that had been trapped in a spit hood that was in place over his face.

On Saturday, the jury of eight men and four women at the trial in Nova Scotia Supreme Court sent notes seeking clarification from Justice Kevin Coady on his charge to them three times over the course of the day.

The judge brought them back into court and read again from a portion of his instructions, particularly a part where they must consider whether the offence involved the defendants doing something or omitting to do something that is within their duty to do and whether it "shows wanton or reckless disregard for the lives and safety of others."
Gardner and Fraser are accused of failing to properly conduct safety checks on Rogers every 15 minutes while he was under their watch.

In the afternoon, the jury sent a note to the judge saying that they were not unanimous in their views on part of the judge's instructions that said the Crown must prove that the defendants' actions were "a marked and substantial departure from the standard of care or a reasonable person in the circumstances."
Coady had earlier clarified that "reasonable person" would refer to another booking officer.

Crown attorney Chris Vanderhooft submitted that there was confusion related to the judge's instructions and suggested he introduce new instructions using a clearer standard set out in David Watt's Manual of Criminal Jury Instructions.
"If you don't explain the test that applies in a way that they can apply it, then that is going to be an error in law," Vanderhooft told the judge.
But Gardner's lawyer David Bright stood and suggested the jury was deadlocked.
Coady brought the jury back in and asked them to pause deliberations while he reassessed his instructions.
Vanderhooft submitted that the Watts version of instructions provided a clearer order of decision-making that the jury might find easier to understand
Again, Bright disagreed.
"We're all guessing as to what they really want to know," he said. "My respectful submission is that if we read all of Watts, we may as well have a mistrial and have a new trial with a full charge."

When Coady brought the jury back in, he read them the more extensive Watts instructions, which slightly rearranged the order in which they should consider their decisions and sent them back to deliberations.

Shortly before 5 p.m., the jury sent another note, this time asking for written copies of the Watts instructions. Coady agreed to provide them but then decided to sequester them once more and pick things up in the morning.
Including Friday's deliberations, the jury has been working on a decision for almost 10 hours.

Rogers was arrested outside the IWK children's hospital that night, with one arresting officer testifying that he saw the 41-year-old man, whose girlfriend had just given birth to their child at the IWK, down a half-pint of Fireball whiskey before being taken into custody.

During the course of the trial, the jury heard that HRP constables Ryan Morris, Justin Murphy and Donna Paris had to carry Rogers into the booking area shortly before 11 p.m. and had applied a spit hood to his head to prevent him from spitting on anyone.
They dragged him into a Cell 5 and removed his handcuffs but left the spit hood in place.

Gardner and Fraser did conduct some checks but they limited their activity to stopping at the door of the cell and observing whether Rogers was in distress or not. The jury heard that there was a policy in place, referred to as the "Four-Rs," that requires booking officers to check for "rousability, response to a question, response to command, and remembering."

Under this policy, they were supposed to enter the cell and try to wake the prisoner up. Gardner, Fraser and veteran booking officer Stephan Longtin testified during the trial that shortage of staff, workloads and safety concerns were factors in the commonplace decision among booking officers to not enter a cell alone.
The proceedings are to resume Sunday morning at 9 a.m.
